title: The past tense
intro: Every verb so far has been in the present continuous. This unit adds the past tense `-DI`, the one you use for things that happened and are over: *Dün ne yaptın?* (What did you do yesterday?) *Sinemaya gittim* (I went to the cinema). It brings a second set of personal endings, which you'll compare with the first, and the time words that go with the past.

blocks.text: The past tense (*görülen geçmiş zaman*, the witnessed past) is built in three pieces: the stem, `-DI`, and a personal ending: *gel-* + *-di* + *-m* → *geldim* (I came). It tells what happened, usually something you saw or did yourself.

blocks.label: Past tense
lines: D → d   after vowels and voiced consonants
D → t   after f, s, t, k, ç, ş, h, p
I       four-way harmony with the stem

blocks.text: The D behaves exactly like the D of the locative in [A1 unit 5](gp-consonant-assimilation): *geldi*, *okudu*, but *yaptı*, *içti*, *gitti*. The I follows four-way harmony with the last vowel of the stem: *geldi*, *aldı*, *okudu*, *gördü*.

**The stem never changes.** Because `-DI` starts with a consonant, nothing softens and no vowel drops, unlike with `-(I)yor`: *gitti* (but *gidiyor*), *bekledi* (but *bekliyor*), *yedi* (but *yiyor*), *dedi* (but *diyor*).

blocks.title: *yapmak* (to do): p is voiceless, so the D becomes t

items.en: Yesterday evening I watched a film.
Ayşe wrote a letter to her mother.

items.en: At the weekend I read a very good book.
We went to the cinema yesterday.
What did you do at the weekend?

blocks.text: The ending for **we** is *-k*, not `-(y)Iz`: *geldik*, *yaptık*. And **you** (plural or polite) is `-nIz`: *geldiniz*, never *geldisiniz*. You'll see why in the third section.

blocks.title: I'm hungry: acıktım
blocks.text: Some changes of state are said in the past, where English uses the present: *Acıktım* (I'm hungry: I have got hungry), *Susadım* (I'm thirsty), *Yoruldum* (I'm tired), *Geç kaldım* (I'm late), *Anladım* (I see, got it), *Bitti* (It's over).

sections.title: Gelmedim, geldin mi? Negative and questions

blocks.text: **Negative.** Put `-mA` between the stem and `-DI`: *gel-* + *-me-* + *-di* + *-m* → *gelmedim* (I didn't come). This `-mA` has two-way harmony, e or a, unlike the `-mI` of *gelmiyor*. Since it ends in a vowel, the D after it is always d: *gitmedi*, *yapmadı*.

**Questions.** Here the past works the other way round from `-(I)yor`: the personal ending stays on the verb, and `mI` comes last, as a separate word in harmony with the vowel before it: *Geldin mi?* (Did you come?), *Okudun mu?*, *Gördün mü?*, *Yaptınız mı?* Compare *Geliyor musun?*, where the ending moves onto the particle.

items.en: Have you eaten? Did you eat?
I didn't understand. Sorry, I didn't catch that.

blocks.text: A short answer repeats the verb: *Geldin mi? Evet, geldim.* or *Hayır, gelmedim.*
Never move the ending onto the particle with `-DI`: *geldin mi?*, not *geldi misin?*; *yaptınız mı?*, not *yaptı mısınız?* For **they**, *-lAr* stays on the verb too: *geldiler mi?*

English needs **did** for questions and negatives, and often uses **have** for recent events. Turkish `-DI` covers them all: *Yemek yedin mi?* is both **Did you eat?** and **Have you eaten?**, and *Anahtarımı kaybettim* is **I lost my key** or **I've lost my key**.

Turkish verbs take one of two main sets of personal endings. You learned the first in [A1 unit 3](gp-copula-present) with **to be** and used it in [A1 unit 6](gp-present-continuous) with `-(I)yor`. The past tense brings the second. Turkish grammars call them *zamir kökenli* (from the pronouns, as `-(y)Iz` recalls *biz*) and *iyelik kökenli* (from the possessive suffixes); English-language grammars say type I and type II, or the z-type and the k-type, after their endings for **we**.

blocks.caption: Which forms take which set
head: Endings
Forms that take them
rows: present of **to be** (*öğrenciyim*), present continuous (*geliyorum*), and later the [future](gp-future) (*geleceğim*), the [aorist](gp-aorist-forms) (*gelirim*), [-mIş](gp-mis-intro) (*gelmişim*) and [-mAlI](gp-meli) (*gelmeliyim*)
past `-DI` (*geldim*), and later the [past of to be](gp-past-copula) (*öğrenciydim*) and the [conditional](gp-conditional-sa) (*gelsem*)

blocks.text: Two things help you keep them apart. Type II endings look like the possessive suffixes of [A1 unit 9](gp-possessive-suffixes): *evim, evin* and *geldim, geldin*. And in a question, type I endings move onto `mI` (*geliyor musun?*), while type II endings stay on the verb (*geldin mi?*).
Don't mix the two sets on one verb: *geldik*, not *geldiyiz*; *geldiniz*, not *geldisiniz*; *geldin*, not *geldisin*.

The imperative of [A1 unit 12](gp-imperative) has persons of its own (*gel, gelin*), and so will the [optative](gp-optative) and the [third-person imperative](gp-imperative-3rd) later in A2. Learn each set with the form that takes it.

sections.title: Yesterday, last week, two days ago

blocks.text: These time words go with the past. Like all time words, they usually come at the start of the sentence or right after the subject.

**… önce, ago.** Put *önce* after a number and a time word: *üç gün önce*, *beş dakika önce*, *on yıl önce*. After a number the noun stays singular, as in [A1 unit 11](gp-numbers-singular): *iki gün önce*, never *iki günler önce*. (*Önce* after the ablative, *yemekten önce*, means **before**; that comes in [unit 9](gp-postp-ablative).)

**Not yet: henüz, daha.** With a negative verb, *henüz* and *daha* both mean **not yet**; *daha* is more colloquial: *Henüz gelmedi* or *Daha gelmedi* (He hasn't come yet). With a positive verb, *henüz* means **just**: *Henüz geldim* (I've only just arrived).
**Already: zaten.** *Zaten* means **already**, or **anyway** when it backs up what you say: *Zaten yedim* (I've already eaten), *Zaten geç kaldık* (We're late anyway).

items.en: Last week we went to Izmir.
I went to sleep very late last night.

blocks.text: English puts **not yet** and **already** with the present perfect: **I haven't eaten yet**, **I've already eaten**. Turkish keeps the ordinary past, much as French uses its passé composé for both I ate and I have eaten: *Henüz yemedim*, *Zaten yedim*.
*Önce* follows the time phrase, like English **ago**: *iki gün önce*, not *önce iki gün*. And *geçen* comes before the noun: *geçen hafta*, **last week**.

summary: The past tense is stem + `-DI` + a type II ending: *geldim, geldin, geldi, geldik, geldiniz, geldiler*.
D becomes t after f, s, t, k, ç, ş, h, p (*yaptım*, *gitti*), and the I follows four-way harmony (*aldı, okudu, gördü*).
In a past question the ending stays on the verb and `mI` comes last: *Geldin mi?*, *Yaptınız mı?*
Type I endings (`-(y)Im, -sIn, -(y)Iz, -sInIz`) go with **to be** and `-(I)yor`; type II (`-m, -n, -k, -nIz`) with `-DI`.
Time words: *dün*, *geçen hafta*, *iki gün önce*; *henüz* or *daha* + negative for **not yet**; *zaten* for **already**.
